newsitem.title: CHINA: HK stocks soar then slump at start of China era.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks soar then slump at start of China era.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks went on a wild ride on Thursday as remnants of the festive handover mood pushed the Hang Seng Index to a record high before the sobering reality of the property market pulled investors back down to earth.

The blue chip index closed the first trading day under Chinese rule down 141.05 points, or 0.93 percent, at 15,055.74 after handover enthusiasm pushed the index to an all-time high of 15,363.61 during early trade.
The red chip China-Affiliated Corporations Index fell 55.82 points, or 1.61 percent, to 3,413.50 after rising to its highest level since its launch last month at 3,569.27 in early trade.
"Handover fever is coming to an end and investors are taking a break in the short run before taking new positions," said Edwin Cheung, a senior sales manager at Taiwan Securities.
The market reopened for trade on Thursday after a holiday on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday to mark Hong Kong's reversion to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
The Hang Seng Index ended the final day of trading under British rule last Friday at an all-time closing high of 15,196.79 points.
"It was strong before the handover and you have a bit of a morning-after effect," said Richard Verin, head of equities trading at CS First Boston.
"There is always a little bit of volatility after a big event. The market tries to find the level at which it should be trading. It is a bit of price discovery."

Analysts expected a period of consolidation for share prices in coming days, with soft property stocks likely to dampen sentiment after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said in his inaugural address on Tuesday that his new administration would increase housing supply to tackle high property prices.
While specific policy details are still unknown, uncertainty is likely to weigh on the property sector, analysts said.

"Profit-taking pressures will limit the upside in the short term and property stocks will remain under pressure since investors are still unclear about government policy," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.

Analysts said retail investors had been responsible for the market's drive into record ground within the first few minutes of trade on Thursday, but institutional investors had been more inclined to reduce positions and turn to Thailand, where the de facto devaluation of the baht had made equities more attractive.
"Over the next few days this round of selling will be completed," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
"Hopefully when this round of selling by institutional investors is completed the market can move up again."
Verin said the market could see more volatility over coming months after reaching new highs.
"The market is having trouble around these levels," he said, predicting a range of 14,400 to 15,400 points in the near term.

But with the backdrop of solid earnings growth and steady interest rates following the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision this week to leave interest rates unchanged, analysts expected more records ahead.

"The solid fundamentals of the top Hong Kong listed companies are beyond dispute," Mansion House Research said in its daily report, putting its index target for the second half of the year at 16,400 points.
Kelvin Tang, an analyst at ImPac Asset Management, said a continued strong flow of mainland money into the Hong Kong market would also help lift prices.
"I expect the market will consolidate a bit and then go up again because of the liquidity," he said.
